title: Between the two
hook: when they spend, neither wasteful nor stingy, but in between (25:67)

segments.voice: Yesterday, hawnan, they walk humbly, and your line was to walk gently and say peace. Did someone test it? What did you say? Day four hundred ninety-nine.

There are two kinds of people who are hard to go shopping with. One buys everything, the second pair of shoes, the upgrade, the thing that was on sale, and checks the bank balance with one eye closed. The other won't buy a sandwich, counts every coin twice, and somehow makes everyone around them feel guilty for eating. Some people manage to be both in the same week. The portrait of the servants of the Merciful continues, and one of its strokes is about money.
screen: `THE ONE WHO WON'T BUY A SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-seven. Pickthall: "And those who, when they spend, are neither prodigal nor grudging; and there is ever a firm station between the two". Prodigal is israf, going past the limit, spending beyond what's needed or right. Grudging is qatr, tightening, squeezing, holding back what ought to be given. And between them, qawam. Pickthall calls it a firm station. It's from the same root as standing upright, qama. Qawam is the place where something stands steady, balanced, not tipping either way. So the middle here isn't lukewarm. It's upright. Another surah gives the same picture with a body: don't keep your hand chained to your neck, and don't stretch it out all the way either. And there's a moment in Bukhari that shows what the middle looks like in a real decision. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas was ill and thought he might die. He was wealthy, with one daughter as his heir. He asked the Prophet ﷺ if he could give two-thirds of his wealth away in charity. No, he was told. Half? No. A third? A third, the Prophet said, and a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them dependent on other people. Even generosity has a middle. The question isn't only, am I giving enough? It's also, am I keeping enough for the people I'm responsible for? The firm station is where both questions get a fair answer. And it isn't a single number. It moves with your life.
screen: `ISRAF: GOING PAST THE LIMIT.` · `QATR: SQUEEZING TIGHT.` · `QAWAM: STANDING UPRIGHT BETWEEN.` · `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one purchase. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of something you bought this week, or are about to buy. Ask two questions. Is this past what I need, or what's right? And on the other side: am I holding back somewhere I should be giving, to myself, to my family, to someone in need? Don't scold yourself. Just look for where the firm middle would stand. The bell holds the time.
Qawam. A firm, upright station between prodigal and grudging spending, standing steady, not tipping either way. Today's word.
Your line: in between. Today, before one purchase, pause and ask whether it's past the limit, or whether you're squeezing too tight. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 25:67 and 17:29 on balanced spending, and Islamic law generally limits bequests to one third of an estate, following the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

match.prompt: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

original.note: Arabic: qawam, a firm, upright middle; from the root of qama, to stand.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't spend too much.
what it means: don't spend past the limit, and don't squeeze tight either; stand upright between the two.
what a scholar hears: israf and qatr as the two extremes, qawam from q-w-m; compare 17:29; the one-third limit on bequests derives from the hadith of Sa'd (Bukhari 2742).
